rationale: A wins because it knows where the facts stop. Its line "the angle is the *unverifiability* of the number, not the number as a triumph" is a real reporting lens; B keeps stapling conclusions onto thin facts with "puts a newsletter platform in the ring with YouTube and TikTok" and "The numbers behind Substack's \"struggling platform\" reputation don't add up." That is not strategy, it is importing a fight and a verdict the update does not prove.
gaps_in_A: "Substack is spending on a media-app build while privately held and short on funding" overstates the supplied fact. The update says public funding struggles, not that Substack is currently short on funding.

"the same cut now extending over video and podcast monetization" is too confident. The facts say Substack takes 10% of subscription revenue and video/podcasts can be monetized; they do not prove identical economics for video and podcast products.
"the YouTube/Patreon/Substack competitive set" is a mild imported frame. A mostly contains it with a proof warning, but the facts name no competitor.
gaps_in_B: "Substack completes its swap from email newsletter to all-in-video media app" is headline overreach. Native video plus a media-app strategy is not a completed swap, and "all-in-video" is invented.
"puts a newsletter platform in the ring with YouTube and TikTok" invents a competitive war. A TikTok-style feed is not evidence that Substack is directly taking on YouTube or TikTok.
"a short-form, algorithmic-style feed" is unsupported. The update says TikTok-style feed; it does not say short-form, algorithmic, or video-first.

"The numbers behind Substack's \"struggling platform\" reputation don't add up" is bad math in a trench coat. Creator earnings and paid subscriptions do not, by themselves, answer Substack's funding, revenue, or profitability questions.
